questions.e: A state machine model can be derived from the specification, from the code (also using reverse engineering techniques), or from both.

questions.q: For a stack class with a maximum capacity of 10, which state is defined as the number of elements being greater than 0 but less than the maximum capacity?
o: Empty
Full
Holding
Initial
questions.e: The stack's states are Initial (before creation), Empty (elements = 0), Holding (elements > 0 but less than max), Full (elements = max), and Final (after destruction). 'Holding' is the partially-filled state.

questions.q: In the stack example, under what condition does the 'add' action move the stack directly from the Empty state to the Full state?
o: Whenever delete is called
If the stack size is 10
If the maximum capacity is 1
Only during destruction
questions.e: Empty -> Holding is normally caused by 'add', but Empty -> Full via 'add' occurs only if the maximum capacity is 1, so a single add fills the stack completely.

questions.q: In the stack example, which transition takes the stack from Holding back to Empty, and under what condition?
o: 'create' when size = max
'add' when size = 0
'delete' when the size is 1
'destroy' when size > 1
questions.e: Holding -> Empty is caused by the 'delete' action when s.size() = 1, i.e. removing the last remaining element empties the stack.

questions.q: According to the definition given, what are the components of a test case?
o: Only inputs and expected outputs
Pre-condition, inputs, test sequence, expected output and/or pass/fail criteria, and post-condition
Trigger, guard, and activity
State, transition, and coverage metric
questions.e: A test case is defined as a pre-condition, inputs, a test sequence, an expected output and/or pass/fail criteria, and a post-condition.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a coverage criterion for state-based testing?
o: All statements covered
All events forced to occur at least once
All def-use pairs covered
All branches covered
questions.e: The state-based coverage criteria are: all states (pass through all states), all events (force all events to occur at least once), and all actions (force all actions to be produced at least once). Statement, branch, and def-use are structural/code criteria, not state-based ones.

questions.q: In the fault model, what characterizes an incorrect 'transition' fault versus an 'event' fault?
o: A transition fault means the output differs from the specified one
A transition fault means the new state is legal but incorrect, while an event fault means a valid message is ignored
Both mean an extra state is created
A transition fault means a valid message is ignored
questions.e: A transition fault means the new state is legal but incorrect, whereas an event fault means a valid message is ignored. These are distinct entries under 'missing or incorrect'.

questions.q: How is a 'sneak path' defined?
o: A transition that is never executed
A duplicated test case
A message that is accepted when it should not be accepted
A state that has no outgoing transitions
questions.e: A sneak path is a message accepted when it should not be; it can occur if there is an unspecified transition or if a transition occurs even though its guard predicate is false.

questions.q: In the transition form 'trigger-signature [guard] / activity', what does the guard represent?
o: A Boolean condition that must be true for the transition to take place
The event that triggers a potential change of state
The resulting state after the transition
An action performed during the transition
questions.e: In trigger-signature [guard] / activity, the trigger-signature is the event, the guard is a Boolean condition that must be true for the transition to occur, and the activity is the action performed during the transition.

questions.q: How is a round-trip path tree constructed, and what does it include?
o: From source code; it includes all statements
From a state transition diagram; it includes all round-trip paths
From a control-flow graph; it includes all basis paths
From a data-flow graph; it includes all def-use paths
questions.e: A round-trip path tree is built from a state transition diagram and includes all round-trip paths (transition sequences that begin and end in the same state) plus simple paths from initial to final state; if a loop is present only one iteration is used.

questions.q: What is a 'fault model' as used in model-based testing?
o: A record of all faults already fixed in the code
A hypothetical model of what types of faults may occur in an implementation
A tool that automatically repairs faults
A list of hardware failures
questions.e: A fault model is a hypothetical model of what types of faults may occur in an implementation; most fault models are 'structural', being a refinement of the specification formalism (e.g. mutations of the specification or of a correct implementation).

questions.q: In the fault model for finite state machines, what is a 'transfer fault'?
o: A transition is added or missing
The machine becomes non-deterministic
The machine provides an output different from the one specified
The machine enters a different state than that specified by the transfer function
questions.e: A transfer fault occurs when the machine enters a different state than the one specified by the transfer function. This is distinct from an output fault, where the machine gives an output different from that specified by the output function.

questions.q: In the FSM fault model, the fault of 'additional or missing transitions' arises from violating which basic assumption?
o: That the FSM is deterministic and completely (fully) specified
That every state has a self-loop
That the FSM has exactly one final state
That the FSM is written in Java
questions.e: One basic assumption is that the FSM is deterministic and completely defined (fully specified); additional or missing transitions represent faults where it turns out to be non-deterministic and/or incompletely (partially) specified.

questions.q: In conformance testing, what does the 'controllability' limitation refer to?
o: The IUT cannot be directly put into a desired state, usually requiring several additional state transitions
The test takes an unacceptably long time to run
The tester cannot observe the internal state of the IUT
The IUT rejects all inputs
questions.e: Controllability is the limitation that the Implementation Under Test cannot be directly placed into a desired state, usually requiring several additional state transitions. Observability, by contrast, is the inability to directly observe the IUT's state.

questions.q: In conformance testing, what does the 'observability' limitation prevent?
o: The tester from directly observing the state of the IUT, which is critical to detect errors
The IUT from being placed into a desired state
The FSM from being deterministic
The test suite from being reused
questions.e: Observability prevents the external tester from directly observing the state of the IUT, which is critical for a test to detect errors; controllability is the separate problem of not being able to force the IUT into a desired state.

questions.q: What does a 'model' mean in the context of model-based testing?
o: A physical prototype of the hardware
An exact copy of the implementation
A description of a system's behavior that is simpler than the system it describes
A list of test cases
questions.e: A model is a description of a system's behavior; models are simpler than the systems they describe and help us understand and predict system behavior. Examples used for testing include state machines and specifications such as UML diagrams.

questions.q: In FSM-based formal conformance testing using a black box approach, what is observable to the external tester?
o: The internal states of the IUT
The transfer function of the IUT
Only the outputs generated by the IUT upon receipt of inputs
The source code of the IUT
questions.e: In the black box approach, only the outputs generated by the IUT (upon receipt of inputs) are observable to the external tester; the internal state is not directly visible.

questions.q: Which representation is explicitly stated to be NOT under consideration as a model in model-based testing?
o: UML use case and sequence diagrams
State machines
Control-flow graphs (CFG) and data-flow graphs (DFG)
Object-Z formal specifications
questions.e: Models considered include UML artefacts (use case, sequence, state-charts, class), mathematical representations (Z, VDM, Object-Z), and graphical ones (graph transformation systems, state machines). It is explicitly noted that CFG, DFG etc. are not under consideration here.

questions.q: The 'promising' relation between a model and the System Under Test (SUT) is stated as which of the following?
o: If the model is formal, then the SUT is bug-free
If the SUT passes all tests, then no model is needed
If the SUT compiles, then the model is correct
If there is a transformation sequence possible in the model, then there is a corresponding such sequence in the SUT
questions.e: The relation should be promising: IF there is a transformation sequence possible in the model, THEN there is a corresponding such sequence in the SUT. This lets test cases drawn from the model be applied to the SUT.

questions.q: In the shopping-cart state machine example, how many purchases must customers make in one go before the system moves toward verifying payment details and the delivery address?
o: Fifteen
Five
Ten
Twenty
questions.e: The requirement states customers have to make ten purchases in one go, after which the system allows them to verify their payment details and delivery address; the diagram shows the transition guarded by #(Item) = 10.

questions.q: In the shopping-cart example test suite, the sequence 'Idle -> Identify User -> Idle' (returning to Idle) was identified as evidence of what?
o: A valid successful login
A missing final state
A possible sneak path found due to lack of a system check
An output fault
questions.e: That test row is labelled a possible sneak path, found due to lack of a system check; sequences such as Idle -> Identify User -> Idle and Select Item -> Select item illustrate transitions accepted when they should not be.

questions.q: When wrapping up model-based testing with FSMs, the finalized coverage metric was that which paths must be covered?
o: Only round-trip paths
Only the shortest path from initial to final state
Only paths without loops
All sneak paths, all trap doors, and all paths
questions.e: The finalized coverage was that all sneak paths, all trap doors, and all paths must be covered, and test scenarios then consider all positive and all negative cases.

questions.q: After individual units have been combined into (sub-)modules, what two things does integration testing primarily aim to assure?
o: That every statement and branch within each unit has been executed
That the system meets its port input and output timing constraints
That the units are following the design accurately and are collaborating properly
That each unit meets its documentation and tooling requirements
questions.e: Integration testing checks combined units to confirm they follow the design accurately and collaborate properly. Test/documentation/tool requirements belong to the unit test strategy, and statement/branch coverage is a unit-level concern.

questions.q: In top-down integration based on functional decomposition, what mechanism replaces lower-level classes (such as corporate customer and personal customer) that are not yet ready?
o: MM-paths
Stubs
Call graphs
Drivers
questions.e: Top-down integration proceeds from the top of the decomposition tree; not-yet-ready lower classes are replaced by stubs, which are 'called' programs (fake classes) used just to test. Drivers are the counterpart used in bottom-up integration.

questions.q: How is a stub described in the context of top-down integration?
o: A directed graph whose nodes are units
A 'called' program, i.e. a fake class created just to test
A routine that requires a subsystem and passes a test case to it
A control program that arranges test case input and output
questions.e: A stub is a 'called' program, a fake class used just to test. The control program that arranges test input/output and the routine that passes a test case to a subsystem both describe a driver, used in bottom-up integration.

questions.q: One reason for keeping actual code out and continuing to use a stub even after the real class is ready is:
o: To convert the process into a big-bang strategy
For fault localization
To make fault isolation harder for auditing purposes
To reduce the number of drivers required
questions.e: Stubs are replaced with actual code either when ready or when desired; keeping the actual code out is done deliberately for fault localization. The other options misattribute unrelated goals.

questions.q: Which of the following is identified as a difficulty when writing stubs for functional-decomposition-based integration?
o: Fewer stubs than drivers are typically required
Writing stubs is difficult when parameter passing is complex, and stubs must allow all possible conditions to be tested
Stubs may be more complicated than drivers
Stubs test the most important subsystem (UI) last
questions.e: Writing stubs is difficult when parameter passing is complex, and stubs must allow all possible conditions to be tested. Testing the UI last is a bottom-up issue, and typically fewer drivers than stubs (not the reverse) are required.

questions.q: The number of stubs required can become high specifically when:
o: The top level of the system contains many functional units
The system is object-oriented
Parameter passing is simple
The lowest level of the system contains many functional units
questions.e: The number of stubs may become high when the lowest level of the system contains many functional units, since each must be stubbed out during top-down integration.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the bottom-up integration strategy?
o: It tests units at the lowest levels first and gradually includes subsystems that reference previously tested subsystems
It restricts each testing session to a single pair of units in the call graph
It tests the top subtree first and works downward using stubs
It combines top-down and bottom-up in a single pass
questions.e: Bottom-up integration tests the lowest-level units first, then repeatedly incorporates subsystems that require previously tested subsystems until all are included. Combining both directions describes sandwich, and pair-restriction describes pair-wise integration.

questions.q: In bottom-up integration, a driver is best described as:
o: A directed edge between two units in a call graph
A stored data value that is not immediately used
A fake routine that requires a subsystem and passes a test case to it
A fake class that is called by higher-level units
questions.e: A driver is a 'fake' routine that requires a subsystem and passes a test case to it; the driver (control program) arranges test case input and output. A fake called class is a stub.

questions.q: Why is bottom-up integration considered not optimal for functionally decomposed systems?
o: It cannot use the notions of stubs and drivers
It always deteriorates into a big-bang strategy
It tests the most important subsystem (the UI) last
It requires more drivers than stubs
questions.e: Bottom-up integration is not optimal for functionally decomposed systems because it tests the most important subsystem, the UI, last. It is, however, more useful for integrating object-oriented systems.

questions.q: Comparing drivers and stubs in integration testing, which statement holds?
o: Stubs may be more complicated than drivers, and fewer stubs are required
Drivers are only used in top-down integration
Drivers and stubs are always equal in number and complexity
Drivers may be more complicated than stubs, and fewer drivers than stubs are typically required
questions.e: Drivers may be more complicated than stubs, yet typically fewer drivers than stubs are required. Drivers are associated with bottom-up integration, not top-down.

questions.q: Sandwich integration is characterized by which combination of properties?
o: It uses only drivers and tests the UI first, with easy fault isolation
It eliminates stubs and drivers entirely by using the call graph
It restricts each session to a pair of units to avoid big-bang testing
It combines top-down with bottom-up, needs less stub and driver development effort, but adds difficulty in fault isolation
questions.e: Sandwich integration combines the top-down strategy with the bottom-up strategy, reducing stub and driver development effort, at the cost of added difficulty in fault isolation.

questions.q: According to the guidance on reporting faults, when should a fault be reported?
o: Only after the fault has been replicated/duplicated so that it occurs every time given certain inputs
Only when a stub has been replaced by actual code
Only after all subsystems have been integrated
As soon as any unexpected output is observed once
questions.e: A fault should be reported only after it has been replicated or duplicated, meaning it occurs every time in every usage when certain inputs are provided, making it reproducible.

questions.q: In call graph based integration testing, what do the nodes and edges of a call graph represent?
o: Nodes are messages and edges are module execution paths
Nodes are ASFs and edges are port events
Nodes are test cases and edges are stubs
Nodes are units and edges correspond to actual program calls (or messages)
questions.e: A call graph is a directed graph whose nodes are units and whose edges correspond to actual program calls (or messages) between those units.

questions.q: The relationship between a program's call graph and its functional decomposition tree is that the call graph:
o: Would equal the functional decomposition tree only in the worst case
Has more nodes than the decomposition tree by definition
Can never resemble the decomposition tree
Is always identical to the decomposition tree
questions.e: The call graph would be equal to the functional decomposition tree only in the worst case, because edges reflect actual calls rather than the full hierarchical structure.

questions.q: In pair-wise integration, how many integration test sessions result and why is each session restricted to a pair of units?
o: One session per node, to reduce driver effort
One session for each edge in the call graph, so the process does not deteriorate into a big-bang strategy
One session for the whole graph, to eliminate stubs and drivers
Two sessions per neighborhood, to ease fault isolation
questions.e: Pair-wise integration uses actual code instead of stubs/drivers, restricting each session to a pair of units so the process does not deteriorate into a big-bang strategy; the result is one integration test session for each edge in the call graph.

questions.q: What is the stated objective of pair-wise integration?
o: To use actual code instead of stubs/drivers, eliminating the need to develop them
To create one test session per neighborhood
To test the UI subsystem last
To combine top-down and bottom-up strategies
questions.e: Pair-wise integration eliminates the need for developing stubs/drivers; its objective is to use actual code instead of stubs/drivers, one session per edge of the call graph.

questions.q: In neighborhood integration, how is the neighborhood (radius 1) of a node in a directed graph defined?
o: Only the immediate successor nodes of the node
The set of all nodes reachable by any path from the node
The set of all sink nodes in the graph
The set of nodes one edge away, i.e. all immediate predecessor and successor nodes of the node
questions.e: The neighborhood (radius 1) of a node is the set of nodes one edge away; in a directed graph this means all the immediate predecessor nodes and all the immediate successor nodes of the given node.

questions.q: Compared with pair-wise integration, neighborhood integration testing has which trade-off?
o: It requires one test session per edge and no reduction in effort
It eliminates all stub and driver effort and simplifies fault isolation
It reduces the number of test sessions but makes fault isolation harder
It increases the number of test sessions but makes fault isolation easier
questions.e: Neighborhood integration testing reduces the number of test sessions and reduces stub and driver effort, but fault isolation is harder.

questions.q: A call graph has 5 total nodes of which 4 are sink nodes. Using the neighborhood-size rule shown (total nodes minus sink nodes), what is the neighborhood value?
questions.e: The neighborhood value is computed as total nodes minus sink nodes: 5 - 4 = 1. A graph with 5 nodes and 3 sink nodes would instead give 5 - 3 = 2.

questions.q: In path-based integration, interface-based testing versus interaction-based testing are characterized respectively as:
o: Structural versus behavioral
Both behavioral
Both structural
Behavioral versus structural
questions.e: Interface-based testing is structural while interaction-based testing is behavioral; path-based integration focuses on interactions among units rather than merely testing interfaces, expressing integration in structural and behavioral threads.

questions.q: How is a module execution path defined in path-based integration?
o: A directed edge between two class instantiations
An interleaved sequence of module execution paths and messages
Any path that begins and ends with a port input event
A sequence of statements beginning with a source node and ending with a sink node, with no intervening sink nodes
questions.e: A module execution path is a sequence of statements that begins with a source node and ends with a sink node with no intervening sink nodes. The interleaving of module execution paths and messages defines an MM-path instead.

questions.q: Regarding messages in path-based integration, what distinguishes a synchronous call from an asynchronous call?
o: A synchronous receiver always eventually returns control to the message source, while an asynchronous receiver does not return control to the source
Only asynchronous messages transfer control between units
Only synchronous messages can pass data to other units
A synchronous receiver never returns control, while an asynchronous receiver always returns control
questions.e: By convention, with a synchronous call the unit receiving the message always eventually returns control to the message source, whereas with an asynchronous call it does not return control to the source. Messages of either kind can pass data.

questions.q: An MM-path is defined as:
o: A statement fragment at which program execution terminates
An interleaved sequence of module execution paths and messages that represents a feasible execution path crossing unit boundaries
An action observable at the system level in terms of port input and output events
A directed graph whose edges are program calls
questions.e: An MM-path is an interleaved sequence of module execution paths and messages; MM-paths always represent feasible execution paths and cross unit boundaries. An action observable at the system level in terms of port input and output events instead describes an atomic system function.

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the three observable behavioral criteria that put endpoints on MM-paths?
o: Input quiescence, output quiescence, control quiescence
Event quiescence, message quiescence, data quiescence
Source quiescence, sink quiescence, path quiescence
Port quiescence, module quiescence, unit quiescence
questions.e: The three observable behavioral criteria that serve as natural endpoints for MM-paths are event quiescence, message quiescence, and data quiescence.

questions.q: Message quiescence is said to occur when:
o: A class instantiation calls a method of another class instantiation
A sequence of processing culminates in stored data that is not immediately used
A unit that sends no messages is reached
A system is nearly idle, waiting for a port input event to trigger further processing
questions.e: Message quiescence occurs when a unit that sends no messages is reached. The idle-waiting-for-port-input description is event quiescence, and the stored-but-unused-data description is data quiescence.

questions.q: Data quiescence occurs when:
o: Control is transferred to another unit synchronously
A sequence of processing culminates in the creation of stored data that is not immediately used
A unit that sends no messages is reached
A system waits for a port input event
questions.e: Data quiescence occurs when a sequence of processing culminates in the creation of stored data that is not immediately used, a natural endpoint for an MM-path.

questions.q: An atomic system function (ASF) is defined as an action observable at the system level that:
o: Begins with a source node and ends with a sink node in the same module
Begins with a port input event, traverses one or more MM-paths, and terminates with a port output event
Is an interleaved sequence of module execution paths and messages
Occurs when a unit that sends no messages is reached
questions.e: An atomic system function is observable at the system level in terms of port input and output events: it begins with a port input event, traverses one or more MM-paths, and terminates with a port output event. Test cases exercise ASFs.

questions.q: In the ATM example, which of the following is given as an example of an atomic system function, and which is considered too big to be atomic?
o: Cash dispensing is an ASF; PIN entry would probably be too big (a molecular system function)
PIN entry is an ASF; card entry is too big
Card entry is an ASF; cash dispensing is too big
Session closing is too big; PIN entry is an ASF
questions.e: Examples of an ASF include card entry, cash dispensing, and session closing, whereas PIN entry would probably be too big since it might entail a molecular system function.

questions.q: Confidence-based testing techniques are commonly divided into two families. Which pair correctly names these families?
o: Domain-based techniques and computational techniques
Strong techniques and weak techniques
Structural (coverage-based) techniques and fault-based techniques
Manual techniques and automated techniques
questions.e: Confidence-based testing is split into structural (coverage-based) techniques, whose goodness is judged by how much of the product the test set covers, and fault-based techniques, which instead seek a test set with a high ability to detect faults. Fault seeding and mutation testing are the two fault-based techniques.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three structural (coverage-based) confidence techniques?
o: Mutation coverage
Control-flow coverage
Data-flow coverage
Coverage-based testing of requirements
questions.e: The three structural (coverage-based) techniques are control-flow coverage, data-flow coverage, and coverage-based testing of requirements. Mutation testing is a fault-based technique, not a structural coverage technique.

questions.q: Which two techniques are classified as fault-based (fault-oriented) confidence techniques applicable to all levels of testing?
o: Strong mutation and weak mutation
Fault seeding and mutation testing
Boundary testing and equivalence partitioning
Control-flow coverage and data-flow coverage
questions.e: Fault seeding and mutation testing are the two fault-oriented techniques applicable to all levels of testing. In fault-based testing the artifact structure is not directly considered; instead the aim is a test set with high fault-detection ability.

questions.q: What is the key difference in how faults are introduced by fault seeding versus mutation testing?
o: In fault seeding a predefined number of faults is sown in the code, while in mutation testing exactly one fault is sown at a time, producing an original and a mutant version
Both sow exactly one fault, differing only in the reporting of results
Fault seeding sows faults only in loops, while mutation testing sows faults only in conditionals
In fault seeding exactly one fault is sown, while in mutation testing all possible faults are sown at once
questions.e: In fault seeding a predefined number of artificially generated faults is sown in the program code at once. In mutation testing exactly one fault is sown at a time, yielding the original program and a mutant version of it.

questions.q: In fault seeding and mutation testing, what do the testers know about the artificially generated errors?
o: Nothing; the testers do not know the artificially generated errors
They know the total count in advance
They know the exact location but not the type
They know all of them since they created them
questions.e: The testers do not know the artificially generated errors. The ratio between actual and artificial errors is then examined based on the total number of detected errors, so the seeded faults must be hidden from testers to be meaningful.

questions.q: Which statement about the nature of mutation testing is correct?
o: It outlines specific test data selection criteria
It is a technique for measuring the adequacy of test cases and should be used together with traditional techniques, not instead of them
It is a test-data selection strategy like path or data-flow testing
It replaces traditional testing techniques entirely
questions.e: Mutation testing focuses on measuring the adequacy of test cases. It is NOT a testing strategy like path or data-flow testing and does not outline test data selection criteria, and it should be used in conjunction with traditional techniques rather than instead of them.

questions.q: When is a mutant said to be dead (killed)?
o: When the mutant compiles without error
When a test produces a different result for that mutant than for the original
When no test reaches the mutated statement
When the mutant produces the same output as the original
questions.e: If a test produces different results for one of the mutants, that mutant is said to be dead (killed). A test set that leaves many live mutants is of low quality.

questions.q: If a test set produces D dead mutants out of M total mutants, how is the mutation adequacy score defined, and how should it be interpreted?
o: M/D, where a smaller score means a better test set
D/M, where a larger score means a better test set
M-D, where a larger difference means a better test set
D-M, where a larger difference means a better test set
questions.e: With M mutants and D dead mutants, the mutation adequacy score is D/M. A larger mutation adequacy score means a better test set. The ratio of killed to total mutants (K/M) is likewise a measure of adequacy of the test suite.

questions.q: The mutation score for a set of test cases is the percentage of non-equivalent mutants killed. If D is dead mutants, N is the number of mutants, and E is the number of equivalent mutants, what is the formula?
o: Mutation Score = 100 * D / (N - E)
Mutation Score = 100 * D / N
Mutation Score = 100 * (D - E) / N
Mutation Score = 100 * D / (N + E)
questions.e: Mutation Score = 100 * D / (N - E), where D is dead mutants, N is the number of mutants, and E is the number of equivalent mutants. Equivalent mutants are excluded from the denominator because they can never be killed.

questions.q: A set of test cases is considered mutation adequate when its mutation score equals what value?
o: Any value greater than 0%
questions.e: A set of test cases is mutation adequate if its mutation score is 100%, meaning all non-equivalent mutants have been killed by the test data.

questions.q: What is an equivalent mutant?
o: A mutant produced by two simultaneous syntactic changes
A mutant that fails every test in the suite
A mutant whose fault is never reached by any test
A mutant that still yields the same output as the original even though the statement where the fault was introduced is executed
questions.e: An equivalent mutant arises when the introduction of a fault still yields the same output as the original even though the mutated statement is executed. Because it can never be distinguished from the original, it is excluded (as E) from the mutation score denominator N - E.

questions.q: In the strong-versus-weak distinction, what does strong mutation testing require?
o: That the whole programs P and P' produce different results (all three conditions hold)
Only that the components T and T' produce different results, while P and P' may agree
That no test reaches the mutated statement
That the mutant and original always produce the same output
questions.e: In strong mutation testing, the whole programs P and P' must produce different results, which requires all three conditions to hold. Weak mutation testing only requires that the mutated component T and T' differ (conditions 1 and 2), while P and P' may still produce the same results.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three conditions that must hold for a mutant to be killed under strong mutation testing?
o: A resulting incorrect program state should produce a different output
The mutated statement must never be executed
The mutant must fail to compile
The mutant must differ from the original by two syntactic changes
questions.e: The three conditions are: a test must reach and execute the mutated statement; the input must drive the actual and mutant versions into different states; and the resulting incorrect program state should produce a different output. Only when all three hold (strong mutation) is the mutant killed.

questions.q: The Competent Programmer Hypothesis, an assumption underlying mutation testing, states what?
o: Competent programmers never introduce domain faults
Every program contains exactly one fault
Tests that reveal simple faults can also reveal complex faults
Competent programmers write programs that are approximately correct
questions.e: The Competent Programmer Hypothesis holds that competent programmers write programs that are approximately correct. This is distinct from the Coupling Effect Hypothesis, which claims tests revealing simple faults can also reveal complex faults.

questions.q: The Coupling Effect Hypothesis, an assumption underlying mutation testing, states what?
o: Competent programmers write approximately correct programs
Each mutant must contain multiple faults
Equivalent mutants can always be killed with enough tests
Tests that reveal a simple fault can also reveal complex faults
questions.e: The Coupling Effect Hypothesis holds that tests which reveal a simple fault can also reveal complex faults. This justifies using single-fault mutants to gauge a test suite's ability to detect more complex defects.

questions.q: What is a mutation, as applied to create a mutant program?
o: The deletion of an entire function
A change applied to several statements at once
A change made only to comments and documentation
A single syntactic change made to a program statement
questions.e: A mutation is a single syntactic change made to a program statement. Each mutant differs from the original program by exactly one such mutation, i.e., it contains a single fault.

questions.q: When is a test case considered adequate under the test-adequacy concept?
o: When all mutants generate the same output as the original
When at least one mutant program generates a different output than the original for that test case
When the test case covers 100% of statements
When it detects only seeded faults and no real faults
questions.e: A test case is adequate if it is useful in detecting faults, shown by finding at least one mutant that generates a different output than the original for that test case. If the original and all mutants produce the same output, the test case is inadequate.

questions.q: How can manual mutant creation be automated?
o: By seeding a fixed percentage of domain faults
By running only strong mutation conditions
By computing the confidence value C automatically
Through mutation operators, which are simple changes applied at various program locations
questions.e: Mutation can be automated through mutation operators, which are simple changes that can be made at various program locations. This addresses the problems that manual mutant creation is time-consuming and that a fixed collection of mutants stops being representative of P after many changes.

questions.q: What is identified as the major drawback of mutation testing?
o: The cost of generating the mutants and executing each test case against them
That it always produces equivalent mutants
Its inability to measure test-case adequacy
That it can only be used at the unit level
questions.e: Although theoretical and experimental results show mutation testing is an effective way to measure test-case adequacy, its major drawback is the cost of generating the mutants and executing each test case against every one of them.

questions.q: In fault seeding, if S is the total number of faults seeded, n is the number of seeded faults detected, and N is the number of non-seeded errors detected, the estimated number of remaining (non-seeded) faults in the program is given by which expression?
questions.e: The estimate of remaining non-seeded faults is N(S/n - 1), where S is total seeded faults, n is seeded faults detected, and N is non-seeded errors detected. This assumes seeded faults are detected at the same rate as real ones.

questions.q: Fault seeding as a testing technique is attributed to whom?
o: Mills (1972)
Weyuker (1982)
Dijkstra (1972)
Myers (1979)
questions.e: Fault seeding as a technique was introduced by Mills (1972). It is used to estimate the number of errors remaining in a program by sowing a predefined number of artificial errors.

questions.q: Suppose 100 faults are seeded into a project at time 0. By time 30, 73 of the seeded faults have been detected, and 219 actual (original) faults have been discovered. What is the expected total number of original faults present prior to seeding?
questions.e: The discovered original faults (219) are three times the discovered seeded faults (73). Applying that ratio to the 100 seeded faults gives an expected 300 original faults present before seeding.

questions.q: With 100 faults seeded at time 0, 73 seeded faults detected and 219 original faults discovered by time 30, and an estimated 300 original faults total, how many latent faults are expected to remain at time 30?
questions.e: Latent faults are those remaining and not removed: (300 - 219) = 81 original faults plus (100 - 73) = 27 seeded faults, giving 81 + 27 = 108 latent faults.

questions.q: In fault seeding, if S is the number of seeded faults and s(t) is the number of seeded faults discovered by time t, what does the ratio s(t)/S represent?
o: The number of latent original faults
The seed-discovery effectiveness of testing up to time t
The confidence value C
The mutation adequacy score
questions.e: s(t)/S is the seed-discovery effectiveness of testing to time t. If seeded faults are assumed representative of actual faults, this seed-discovery effectiveness can be taken as representative of overall testing effectiveness.

questions.q: In the fault-seeding confidence formulation where S is the number of seeded faults and N is the total number of non-seeded (indigenous) faults that can be found, when does the confidence C equal 1?
o: When S = 0
When n > N
When N = S
When n < N
questions.e: Confidence is defined as C = 1 if n > N, and C = S/(S - N + 1) if n < N. In the worked mutation/fault-seeding example, C = 1 because N = 0 and n = 2, so n > N.

questions.q: In the worked mutation testing example on myCompute, the original returns a+b when a>b else a-b; mutant M1 changes the guard to a<b and mutant M2 changes a-b to a/b. With 2 dead mutants, 2 total mutants and 0 equivalent mutants, what mutation score results?
questions.e: Using Mutation Score = 100 * D / (N - E) with D = 2 dead mutants, N = 2 mutants, and E = 0 equivalent mutants, the score is 100 * 2/2 = 100%, so the test set is mutation adequate.

questions.q: How do mutation testing and fault seeding compare with respect to system suitability and fault localization?
o: Fault seeding suits critical systems with easy fault localization, while mutation testing is economical but localization is difficult
Both are best only for large systems and neither aids fault localization
Mutation testing suits smaller and critical systems with easy fault localization, while fault seeding is economical but fault localization is difficult
Both are economical and both make fault localization easy
questions.e: Mutation testing is best suited to smaller systems and critical systems, and fault localization is easy. Fault seeding is economical, yet fault localization with it is difficult.

questions.q: How does the mutation adequacy approach differ from fault seeding?
o: It requires that testers know all injected faults in advance
It seeds a predefined number of faults directly into P before testing begins
It estimates the number of remaining faults using N(S/n - 1)
It is applied at a particular point in the testing process, and faults are not directly inserted into P
questions.e: The mutation adequacy approach differs from fault seeding in that it is applied at a particular point in the testing process and in that faults are not directly inserted into P; instead a series of single-fault mutants m(i) are created and the test suite is applied to them.

questions.q: Selenium is best described as which of the following?
o: A set of tools that supports rapid development of test automation for web-based applications
A database engine used to store recorded test results
A single IDE plug-in that only works with Microsoft Visual Studio
A load-generation service that simulates HTTP connections only
questions.e: Selenium is characterized as a set of tools supporting the rapid development of test automation for web-based applications, not a single plug-in, database, or load generator.

questions.q: In what environment does Selenium work?
o: Only where the .NET runtime is installed
Only inside the Selenium IDE application
Only on servers running a specific database
Anywhere JavaScript is supported
questions.e: Selenium works anywhere JavaScript is supported, which is why it is well suited to browser-based web applications.

questions.q: Which set of programming languages is given as being supported by Selenium?
o: Swift, Kotlin, and Objective-C
Java, Ruby, and Python
C, COBOL, and Fortran
SQL, PL/SQL, and T-SQL
questions.e: Selenium is described as supporting languages such as Java, Ruby, and Python.

questions.q: What capability is attributed to Selenium regarding user behavior on web pages?
o: It can rewrite the application's source code automatically
It can only measure server RAM usage per connection
It can simulate a user navigating through pages and then assert for specific marks on the pages
It can only capture screenshots of static pages
questions.e: Selenium can simulate a user navigating through pages and then assert for specific marks on the pages, combining navigation with verification.

questions.q: Once test cases are recorded as a test suite (in Selenium or Visual Studio), what benefit is emphasized about rerunning them?
o: They can only be run once and must then be re-recorded
They can be rerun anytime to see if there is any regression in the overall system quality
They automatically fix any defects they detect
They permanently replace the need for any functional testing
questions.e: A recorded test suite can be run on a click and rerun anytime to check whether there is any regression in the overall system quality.

questions.q: When Selenium is used as an add-on from an IDE such as Visual Studio, how are the recorded test cases executed?
o: By running them using the Selenium driver from inside a test case written in the IDE
By exporting them to a spreadsheet for manual review
By manually retyping each navigation step in the browser
By compiling them into a standalone database script
questions.e: Test cases recorded via an IDE can be executed using the Selenium driver from inside a test case written in the IDE; the worked example uses a test case written in C#.

questions.q: In the web testing checklist, functional testing checks that each component functions as expected, and for that reason it is also referred to by which name?
o: Component testing
Interface testing
Crowd testing
Compatibility testing
questions.e: Functional testing verifies that each component is functioning as expected, and for this reason it is also called component testing.

questions.q: What is the stated aim of compatibility testing within web testing?
o: Ensuring the database maintains data reliability
Ensuring the application works under heavy load
Ensuring how the application is working in the supported environments
Ensuring there is no information leakage in the data
questions.e: Compatibility testing ensures how the application is working across the supported environments, distinguishing it from security, database, and performance testing.

questions.q: Crowd testing is described as which of the following?
o: A large group of perfect strangers trying the product and giving helpful feedback on usability, bugs, and features
Testing the application only under peak concurrent HTTP connections
Testing only the Web Server, Application Server, and Database Server interfaces
Testing that the database maintains data reliability
questions.e: Crowd testing is when a large group of perfect strangers try the product and give phenomenally helpful feedback on usability, bugs, and features.

questions.q: In interface testing, which three areas are identified as needing to be covered?
o: Client browser, DNS server, and load balancer
Throughput, response time, and tuning
Web Server, Application Server, and Database Server
User estimation, load distribution, and activity analysis
questions.e: Interface testing mainly covers three areas: the Web Server, the Application Server, and the Database Server.

questions.q: What is the purpose of security testing as stated in the web testing checklist?
o: To confirm the application works in all supported browsers
To ensure data reliability of the web application's database
To confirm the web application works under a given heavy load
To ensure whether there is any information leakage in terms of encrypting the data
questions.e: Security testing is carried out to ensure whether there is any information leakage, described in terms of encrypting the data.

questions.q: When recording a web test with Microsoft Visual Studio, what is given as one purpose of the recorded test cases?
o: Automatically translating the application into another language
Serving as a record of them for rerunning
Encrypting the application's data at rest
Replacing the need for a production environment
questions.e: A web test recorded with Visual Studio serves many purposes, one being a record of the test cases for rerunning them.

questions.q: How is load testing classified?
o: As a type of non-functional testing
As a type of unit testing
As a type of usability testing
As a type of functional testing
questions.e: Load testing is explicitly categorized as a type of non-functional testing conducted to understand the behavior of the system under test under a specific expected load.

questions.q: A load test is conducted to determine a system's behaviour under which conditions?
o: Only under an idle, zero-user condition
Only under maximum load until it breaks
Only while the source code is being edited
Under both normal and at peak conditions
questions.e: Load testing determines a system's behaviour under both normal and at peak conditions, for a specific expected load.

questions.q: Using the Uber example, user load estimation is primarily concerned with finding out what?
o: Whether the system fails and recovers gracefully
How much RAM and disk quota each connection requires
How the load varies between morning, afternoon, and evening
How many parallel transactions the system under test would support under expected load
questions.e: User load estimation tries to find system behavior under the expected load; the Uber example asks how many parallel transactions the SUT would support.

questions.q: In the Uber example, user load distribution examines system behavior because of what characteristic of usage?
o: Each connection consumes a fixed amount of RAM and disk quota
The user load may peak in the morning or afternoon and be very less in the evening
The system must recover gracefully after being overwhelmed
The database grows bulkier and increases latency over time
questions.e: User load distribution considers that load may peak in the morning or afternoon and be very less in the evening, which also helps determine concurrent and simultaneous users.

questions.q: According to the database size analysis point of load testing, how does database size affect the system?
o: The bulkier the database, the more the latency
Database size has no measurable effect on the load test
The bulkier the database, the less the latency
A larger database reduces the required RAM per connection
questions.e: In database size analysis, the database size does matter: the bulkier the database, the more the latency; DBAs adjust PCT-Used and PCT-Free accordingly.

questions.q: How is stress testing distinguished from load testing?
o: Stress testing examines how the application behaves under maximum load, trying to break the system so it fails and recovers gracefully
Stress testing checks compatibility across supported environments
Stress testing measures response time from the user's perspective under normal load
Stress testing only measures throughput in transactions per second
questions.e: Stress testing examines how an application behaves under maximum load, finding the upper threshold and trying to break the system so it fails and recovers gracefully.

questions.q: For a web application, in what terms is load defined?
o: In terms of the size of the document being edited
In terms of PCT-Used and PCT-Free database settings
In terms of concurrent users or HTTP connections
In terms of RAM and disk quota per user
questions.e: For a web application, load is defined in terms of concurrent users or HTTP connections; the word-processor example (editing a very large document) applies to a different kind of application.

questions.q: Performance testing indicates what, from the user's perspective?
o: The response time for the entire application from the user's perspective
The amount of information leakage in the data
The maximum load at which the application breaks
The number of perfect strangers testing the product
questions.e: A performance test indicates the response time for the entire application from the user's perspective; it is the process of determining speed or effectiveness of a computer, network, program, or device.

questions.q: Which four factors are considered in performance testing?
o: Web Server, Application Server, Database Server, and browser
Usability, compatibility, security, and crowd feedback
Load estimation, load distribution, activity analysis, and database size
Throughput, Response Time, Tuning, and Benchmarking
questions.e: Performance testing considers four factors: Throughput, Response Time, Tuning, and Benchmarking.

questions.q: How is throughput defined in the context of performance testing?
o: The capability of a product to handle multiple transactions in a given period
The system boundaries with respect to number of transactions and parallel connections
The delay between the point of request and the first response from the product
The procedure of enhancing performance by changing parameter values
questions.e: Throughput is the capability of a product to handle multiple transactions in a given period, representing the number of requests or business transactions processed in a specified time duration.

questions.q: How is response time defined?
o: The upper threshold below which the application can work normally
The number of transactions processed per unit of time
The RAM and disk quota required per connection
The delay between the point of request and the first response from the product
questions.e: Response time is defined as the delay between the point of request and the first response from the product.

questions.q: Which performance factor is described as system boundaries with respect to number of transactions, parallel connections, etc.?
o: Throughput
Benchmarking
Response time
Tuning
questions.e: Benchmarking is described as the system boundaries with respect to the number of transactions, parallel connections, and similar limits.

questions.q: What distinguishes tuning as a means of improving product performance?
o: It requires rewriting the product's source code for each parameter
It only applies to the database's PCT-Used and PCT-Free values
It improves performance without having to touch the source code of the product
It measures the delay between a request and the first response
questions.e: Tuning enhances product performance by setting different values for parameters of the product, operating system, and other components, and it improves performance without having to touch the source code.

questions.q: What relationship between web test recording and load testing in Visual Studio is stated?
o: Web test recording is only possible after a load test is created
The same tool used to record a web test is used to come up with a load test
Load testing requires a completely different tool from web test recording
Load testing in Visual Studio can only use Selenium-recorded scripts
questions.e: After recording a web test using Visual Studio, the same tool is used to come up with a load test.

questions.q: System testing is best described as the process of testing which kind of system to verify that it meets its specified requirements?
o: An integrated hardware and software system
A single isolated software module
A collection of unit test drivers and stubs
A control flow graph derived from source code
questions.e: System testing is the process of testing an integrated hardware and software system to verify that the system meets its specified requirements. Individual modules and control-flow constructs are the concern of unit testing, not system testing.

questions.q: What underlying assumption does system testing make before it begins?
o: That unit-level and integration-level testing have already been performed so individual modules are working correctly
That no earlier testing has been done, so all defects must be found at this stage
That only the graphical user interface has been implemented
That the requirements specification is still being written
questions.e: System testing assumes that unit-level testing and integration-level testing have already been performed, and therefore that individual modules are working correctly. Its focus shifts to multi-module functionality, external interfaces and non-functional aspects.

questions.q: In the progression of testing techniques, which techniques are associated with the system testing level?
o: Control flow graph (CFG) and data flow graph (DFG)
MM-Path and call graph
Specification-based and model-based techniques
Functional decomposition and domain testing
questions.e: System testing uses specification-based techniques and model-based techniques. CFG and DFG belong to unit testing, while MM-Path, call graph and functional decomposition belong to integration testing.

questions.q: Which pair of techniques is associated with the integration testing level?
o: MM-Path and call graph
CFG and DFG
Specification-based and model-based techniques
Domain testing and data flow
questions.e: Integration testing techniques include MM-Path, call graph and functional decomposition. CFG and DFG are unit-level techniques, and specification-based and model-based techniques are used at the system level.

questions.q: Which of the following is a NON-functional aspect targeted by system testing?
o: Business processes
Verifying that multi-module functionality meets requirements
Load, stress and volume behavior
System goals
questions.e: Non-functional aspects of system testing include load, stress, volume, performance, security, usability, storage, install-ability, documentation and recovery. Business processes and system goals are functional aspects.

questions.q: In load testing, what is the system subjected to?
o: A set of misuse cases intended to break its security
A statistically calculated load of transactions, processing and parallel connections
An expected volume of stored data such as very large documents
A denial of resources to find where it crashes
questions.e: Load testing subjects the system to a statistically calculated load of transactions, processing, parallel connections and similar demands. Denying resources characterizes stress testing, and handling large data volumes characterizes volume testing.

questions.q: Which tool is given as an example for load testing?
o: PRAL
JMeter
JUnit
ZEROX
questions.e: JMeter is cited as an example tool for load testing. PRAL and ZEROX appear as examples of a backend and affiliated resources in volume testing, not as load-testing tools.

questions.q: Stress testing is described as a form of which other kind of testing?
o: Load testing
Usability testing
Recovery testing
Volume testing
questions.e: Stress testing is described as a form of load testing in which resources are denied in order to find the boundary conditions where the system would crash or become harmful.

questions.q: How are bugs found during stress testing normally handled?
o: They are converted into new functional requirements
They are always repaired immediately before release
They are not normally repaired but reported to the end user for avoidance
They are ignored because stress conditions never occur in practice
questions.e: In stress testing, bugs are not normally repaired; instead they are reported to the end user for avoidance. This reflects that stress conditions probe the system beyond its resource limits.

questions.q: What does performance testing primarily study?
o: Whether the system can store and process very large volumes of data
Whether misuse cases are prevented and use cases are allowed
Performance requirements such as response time and worst, best and average case times to complete operations
Whether HCI principles and de facto standards are followed
questions.e: Performance testing studies performance requirements such as response time and the worst-case, best-case and average-case time to complete a specified set of operations, including transactions per second and memory usage. Misuse cases relate to security, and HCI principles relate to usability testing.

questions.q: Volume testing is intended to determine whether the system can:
o: Handle the expected volume of data, such as a word document with 200,000 pages
Recover after a power failure
Withstand a denial of its resources
Prevent SQL injection attacks
questions.e: Volume testing checks whether the system can handle the expected volume of data, with examples including a backend such as PRAL, affiliated resources such as ZEROX printers, and a word document having 200,000 pages. Resource denial, SQL injection and recovery belong to stress, security and recovery testing respectively.

questions.q: Security testing seeks to confirm that:
o: The system meets its documented usability standards
Use cases are allowed while misuse cases are not allowed
Response times fall within performance requirements
The system can process a large volume of data
questions.e: Security testing aims to verify that use cases are allowed while misuse cases are not, and it is aimed at breaking the system. Specific situations include SQL injections and network security features.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as a specific situation examined during security testing?
o: SQL injections
Handling a 200,000-page document
Verifying HCI principles
Response time measurement
questions.e: Security testing examines specific situations such as SQL injections and network security features. Response time is a performance concern, large-document handling is a volume concern, and HCI principles are a usability concern.

questions.q: Usability and GUI testing verifies which of the following?
o: That HCI principles and documented and de facto standards are properly followed
That misuse cases are blocked
That the system withstands a statistically calculated load
That the system recovers from resource denial
questions.e: Usability and GUI testing verifies that HCI principles are properly followed and that documented and de facto standards are met, using scenarios, questionnaires, user activity logs and inspections.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a method used in usability and GUI testing?
o: SQL injection attempts
Statistically calculated transaction loads
Parallel connection generation
User activity logs
questions.e: Usability and GUI testing uses scenarios, questionnaires, user activity logs and inspections. Parallel connections and transaction loads relate to load testing, while SQL injection relates to security testing.

questions.q: When deriving test cases for the functional aspects of system testing, which four elements are the focus?
o: Data, Action, Device and Event
Valid, Invalid, Not applicable and Boundary
Load, Stress, Volume and Performance
Conditions, Input, Expected result and Actual result
questions.e: For functional aspects, the focus while deriving test cases is on Data, Action, Device and Event. Load, stress and volume are non-functional aspects, and conditions/input/expected/actual are the parameters of a test case in a later step.

questions.q: Which two techniques are described as very widely used for extracting test cases from use cases?
o: MM-Path analysis and call graph analysis
Load simulation and stress simulation
Control flow analysis and data flow analysis
Scenario analysis and test data analysis based on the category partition method
questions.e: The two very used techniques for extracting test cases from use cases are scenario analysis, based on scenario identification, and test data analysis, based on the category partition method.

questions.q: In the four-step process for deriving test cases from use cases, what is the FIRST step?
o: Identify the conditions that cause a test case to execute
Identify the use case scenarios
Add data values to complete each test case
Identify one or more test cases for each scenario
questions.e: The four-step process begins by identifying the use case scenarios; then for each scenario one or more test cases are identified; then the conditions causing execution are identified; and finally the test case is completed by adding data values.

questions.q: In identifying test conditions using a condition matrix, what does marking a condition as 'Valid (V)' mean?
o: It must be true for the basic flow to execute
It represents a boundary value that must be tested
It is not applicable to the test case
It will invoke an alternative flow
questions.e: When stating conditions in the matrix, Valid (V) means the condition must be true for the basic flow to execute, Invalid (I) means it will invoke an alternative flow, and Not applicable (N/A) means it does not apply to the test case.

questions.q: In identifying test conditions, what does marking a condition as 'Invalid (I)' indicate?
o: It will invoke an alternative flow
It must be true for the basic flow to execute
It is not applicable to the test case
It has no effect on which scenario executes
questions.e: Invalid (I) indicates that the condition will invoke an alternative flow, whereas Valid (V) must be true for the basic flow to execute and Not applicable (N/A) means it does not apply to the test case.

questions.q: How does the form of a test case differ across testing levels?
o: A method call at all three levels
A user scenario in unit testing, a single step in integration testing, and a method call in system testing
A sequence of steps in unit testing and a single step in system testing
A single step in unit testing, a sequence of steps in integration testing, and a user/business scenario in system testing
questions.e: A test case is a single step in unit testing, a sequence of steps in integration testing where a step is a method call, and in system testing it is captured as a user/business scenario extracted from use case diagrams and descriptions.

questions.q: In Step 4 of deriving test cases from use cases, which option is offered for designing real input data values?
o: Boundary value analysis
Denial of resources
Data flow graph construction
MM-Path traversal
questions.e: Step 4 designs real input data values to make conditions valid or invalid, with options including looking at use case constructs and branches, considering category-partitioning, and boundary value analysis.

questions.q: What name is given to the scenario matrix used for coverage reporting that lets testers track which test case pertains to which scenario and use-case?
o: Control flow graph
Call graph
Traceability matrix
Context diagram
questions.e: For coverage reporting a scenario matrix is developed and called the traceability matrix, which lets testers track whether sufficient test cases were used and which test case pertains to which scenario and use-case.

questions.q: In the microwave oven use case example, what happens according to the alternate flow when the Cook enters a cooking time equal to zero?
o: The timer immediately signals completion
The system will not start
The system resets its display
The system cooks indefinitely
questions.e: In the microwave oven example, alternate flow 4b states that if the Cook enters a cooking time equal to zero, the system will not start. Other alternate flows describe the door not being closed or no food being placed inside also preventing start.

questions.q: In the microwave oven scenario matrix, the scenario 'Successful Cooking' has which starting and target flows?
o: Starting flow MCA and target flow ACA1
Starting flow MCA and target flow MCA
Starting flow ACA3 and target flow ACA4
Starting flow ACA2 and target flow MCA
questions.e: In the microwave scenario matrix, Scenario 1 (Successful Cooking) has starting flow MCA and target flow MCA, whereas alternate scenarios such as Door Open (MCA to ACA1) and No Food (MCA to ACA2) target different alternate flows.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed among the 'other forms of testing' at the system level?
o: Control flow testing
Data flow testing
Recovery testing
Domain testing
questions.e: Other forms of system testing include storage testing, install-ability testing, documentation testing and recovery testing. Control flow, data flow and domain testing are unit-level techniques.

questions.q: According to the IEEE definition given, verification refers to:
o: Demonstrating that the system is free of all defects
Measuring the worst-case response time under load
Confirming that the software matches the user's implicit expectations
Conformance to examination and provision of objective evidence that specified requirements have been fulfilled
questions.e: The IEEE definition states that verification is conformance to examination and the provision of objective evidence that specified requirements have been fulfilled, which underpins the goal of system testing to verify requirements are met.

questions.q: What is the primary output produced by the test planning activity?
o: The Test Plan document
A traceability matrix only
The Software Requirements Specification
A defect density report
questions.e: Test planning is undertaken to determine the effort needed to validate the quality of the system under test and to engage key stakeholders; its explicit output is the Test Plan document.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the stated purposes of test planning?
o: To eliminate the need for a test environment
To guarantee zero defects in the final product
To replace the SRS document
To ensure testing is a traceable process making efficient use of resources with quantifiable results
questions.e: Test planning is described as essential to ensure testing is a traceable process and to make efficient use of resources while delivering quantifiable results.

questions.q: In test planning, what does 'exit criteria' denote?
o: The number of testers assigned to a project
The list of features not to be tested
The point at which testing must be paused due to instability
Successful completion of a test phase
questions.e: Exit criteria denote the successful completion of a test phase, expressed through measures such as a 100% run rate and an acceptable pass rate. Suspension criteria, by contrast, trigger a pause in testing.

questions.q: How is the 'run rate' used as an exit criterion defined, and what value must it reach?
o: Defects found divided by defects fixed; must be 90%
Test cases executed divided by total test cases; must be 100%
Test cases failed divided by total test cases; must be 0%
Test cases passed divided by test cases executed; must be 100%
questions.e: Run rate is the number of test cases executed divided by the total number of test cases, and it must reach 100% for exit. Pass rate, distinctly, is test cases passed divided by test cases executed.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of a suspension criterion for testing?
o: More than a set number of crashes occurring
The pass rate reaching an acceptable threshold
Achieving a 100% run rate
All requirements being covered in the traceability matrix
questions.e: Suspension criteria trigger a halt to testing, with examples including more than X number of crashes or Y number of test cases reported as failed.

questions.q: According to IEEE Std 829-1983, a test plan is a document describing which of the following?
o: Only the source code structure of the system under test
The defect density and critical-defect percentage
The scope, approach, resources, and schedule of intended testing activities
The command-line options of the testing tool
questions.e: IEEE Std 829-1983 defines the test plan as a document describing the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of intended testing activities, identifying test items, features to be tested, tasks, responsibilities, and risks needing contingency planning.

questions.q: One cited view holds that a test plan is valuable only to a certain extent, beyond which it becomes what?
o: A diversion of resources
A guarantee of quality
A substitute for the SRS
A legally binding contract
questions.e: The Kaner et al. 1999 view states a test plan is valuable to the extent that it helps you manage your testing project and find bugs, and beyond that it is a diversion of resources.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognized section of an IEEE-standard test plan document?
o: Suspension criteria and resumption criteria
Compiler version
Source code repository URL
Marketing budget
questions.e: The IEEE standard test plan structure includes sections such as Test Plan Identifier, Test Items, Features to be tested, Approach, Suspension criteria and resumption criteria, Test deliverables, Responsibilities, Schedule, and Risks and contingencies.

questions.q: The IEEE test plan structure distinguishes between two related feature sections. What are they?
o: 'Features to be tested' and 'Features not to be tested'
'Positive features' and 'Negative features'
'Features tested' and 'Features to be automated'
'Manual features' and 'Automated features'
questions.e: The IEEE test plan explicitly separates 'Features to be tested' from 'Features not to be tested' as two distinct sections.

questions.q: Among the test case ingredients, what is the 'Actual result'?
o: The primary verification point of the test case
What you really get from the application
The unique identifier of the test case
The expected output value defined in advance
questions.e: The actual result is defined as what you really get from the application, which is then compared against the expected result to determine pass or fail. The expected result is the predefined output value.

questions.q: A test case is classified as Positive/Negative and as Manual/Automatable/Automated for what stated purpose?
o: For test execution and general planning purposes
To assign a unique identifier
To record bug numbers for failed cases
To define the pass/fail criteria
questions.e: The Positive/Negative class supports test execution planning, and the Manual/Automatable/Automated parameter is used for planning purposes.

questions.q: How is a tester's motivation distinguished from the motivation behind a test plan?
o: The tester's motivation is to identify all testing aspects, while the test plan's is to find defects
The tester's motivation is to find faults or defects, while the test plan's is to identify all aspects of testing essential to test the SUT
Both share the identical goal of writing documentation
Neither is concerned with the system under test
questions.e: A tester's motivation is to find faults or defects, whereas the test plan's motivation is to provide a mechanism to identify all aspects of testing essential to test the SUT, considering the application domain and SRS document.

questions.q: In the test case lifecycle, what happens to a test case during the 'Review' step?
o: It is executed against the application
It is reviewed periodically or upon a release and then kept as is, updated, or deprecated/deleted
It is created with a new ID
It is always immediately deleted
questions.e: During Review (done periodically or upon a release), a test case is either kept as is, updated and kept for use, or deprecated/deleted depending on the situation.

questions.q: In the state transition of a test case, from which state does it become Blocked, Failed, or Passed?
o: Created
Executed
Untested
Deprecated
questions.e: A test case moves from Untested to Executed, and from the Executed state it can become Blocked, Failed, or Passed.

questions.q: What are the two important characteristics of a test suite?
o: It has exactly four levels, and it excludes performance tests
Its test cases relate to a certain release of the system, and they are organized hierarchically
It contains only automated cases, and it is stored in a spreadsheet
It is created once and never reviewed, and it has no traceability
questions.e: A test suite is a set of test cases organized hierarchically for a certain software release; its two characteristics are that the cases relate to a certain release and that they are organized in a hierarchical manner.

questions.q: What is the purpose of maintaining traceability from the SRS to test documents such as test cases and test suites?
o: To ensure each requirement is covered and thereby establish a measure of completeness while highlighting gaps
To replace the functional specification
To reduce the number of testers needed
To speed up compilation of the code
questions.e: Traceability tracks each software feature from the SRS through to test documents, ensuring each requirement is covered in the functional specification and test cases, which establishes a measure of completeness and highlights gaps.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly lists phases of the Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC)?
o: Test Execution, Test Planning, SUT Analysis, Closure
SUT Analysis, Test Planning, Test case development, Test Environment setup, Test Execution, Test Cycle closure
Requirements, Design, Implementation, Retirement
Coding, Compilation, Deployment, Maintenance
questions.e: The STLC phases are System Under Test (SUT) Analysis, Test Planning, Test case development, Test Environment setup, Test Execution, and Test Cycle closure.

questions.q: Which of the following is described as an input needed to share results once a testing cycle is complete?
o: The source code compiler
The hardware procurement order
The marketing plan
The Test Incident Report, including Test Log, Test Summary Report, Test Metrics, and Coverage Analysis
questions.e: Inputs for test result reporting include the Test Plan document (with design and case specifications), the Test Incident Report (Test Log, Test Summary Report, Test Metrics, Coverage Analysis), and the Program Quality Estimate.

questions.q: Why can documents or spreadsheets not be used for recording test execution results at scale, and what is recommended instead?
o: They cost too much; paper logs are recommended
They are too fast; word processors are recommended
They are inadequate, so bug tracking systems and professional test management software such as Microsoft Test Manager, JIRA, and IBM Rational Test Manager are used
They are only for developers; email is recommended
questions.e: Documents or spreadsheets cannot be used for recording test execution results; small-scale open-source bug tracking tools or professional test management software such as Microsoft Test Manager (MTM), JIRA, and IBM Rational Test Manager are used instead.

questions.q: What core capabilities do bug tracking systems provide to different roles?
o: They let testers report faults and issues, let developers view and fix faults, and let management review progress and perform analysis
They automatically fix all faults without human input
They only let management approve budgets
They only let testers write code
questions.e: Bug tracking systems allow testers to report faults and issues, allow developers to view and fix those faults, and allow management to review progress and perform analysis.

questions.q: In test data management, which artifacts are maintained to help infer information such as product quality metrics and expected completion time?
o: Only the source code
Test oracles, test execution logs, and the traceability matrix
Only the compiler settings
Only the marketing budget
questions.e: Test data management maintains test oracles, test execution resulting data in the form of test execution logs, and the traceability matrix, along with clean-up information and storage of automated test cases, bug logs, and screenshots.

questions.q: Which of the following is cited as a reason test data management is important?
o: Setting the office hours of the QA team
In-process fault arrival for quality assessment, fault predictions, and fault removal effectiveness
Choosing a programming language
Reducing the number of source files
questions.e: Test data management is important for traceability, in-process fault arrival for quality assessment, fault predictions, fault removal effectiveness, and expected test cycle completion.

questions.q: In the described use of Microsoft Test Manager (MTM), how is the tool logged into?
o: Through a web browser only
Through a command-line JAR file
Using Team Foundation Server
By connecting to JIRA
questions.e: MTM is logged into using Team Foundation Server, with a learning management system under development treated as the system under test.

questions.q: When creating a test case in MTM, what two-step approach is described?
o: Delete a requirement, then archive the test case
Set the ramp-up, then set the loop count
Compile the code, then run the sampler
Add a test requirement, then add a test case to test that requirement
questions.e: Creating a test case in MTM involves first adding a test requirement and then adding a test case to test that requirement.

questions.q: In the consolidated test report process, who participates in the meeting that discusses each row of the test execution report?
o: Only the QA lead
Only the automation tools
Only external customers
